With prior $\theta\sim Beta(\alpha,\beta)$ and Bernoulli observations containing $s$ successes and $f$ failures, the likelihood multiplies the prior into $Beta(\alpha+s,\beta+f)$. Thus A has posterior $Beta(11,11)$ and B has $Beta(2,2)$ from uniform priors. Both have mean 0.5, but B has greater uncertainty. [1](https://incompleteideas.net/book/the-book-2nd.html) [2](https://probml.github.io/pml-book/book1.html)

Thompson sampling draws one conversion probability independently from each arm's posterior and selects the arm with the highest draw, then updates after observing its outcome. This naturally balances exploitation and exploration under the model. Account for delayed feedback, changing populations, and the randomization unit in deployment. Equal observed rates do not mean equal evidence, and a stationary Beta–Bernoulli model does not automatically handle drift or contextual differences.
